rashi:a1.1: MISHNA. One who purchases the fetus of his donkey: and it is a firstborn, and it is still in its mother’s womb. And the reason it takes a donkey and not a cow is explained in the second chapter (below, Bekhorot 13a): since the matters of the firstborn donkey are few, the tanna finishes them off and puts them aside, and all the other chapters deal with the firstborn of a kosher animal.
rashi:a1.2: Although he is not permitted: as is taught in tractate Avoda Zara (14b) and in many places: one does not sell them large livestock, because the gentile does labor with it on Shabbat.
rashi:a1.3: And one who enters into a partnership with him: where the two of them put in money between them and buy an animal.
rashi:a1.4: And one who receives an animal from him: where the female donkey belongs to the gentile, and the Jew receives it [to tend] on condition that they divide the offspring; but the body of the female donkey belongs to the gentile.
rashi:a1.5: Is exempt from the firstborn: if that fetus that he bought from the gentile, or that he sold to the gentile, is a firstborn, it is not sanctified, since the gentile has a share in it or in its mother.
rashi:a1.6: As it is stated: “I sanctified to Me every firstborn in Israel” (Numbers 3:13), but not among others, gentiles.
tosafot:a1.1: MISHNA. One who purchases the fetus of a gentile’s donkey, and one who sells to him: the purchaser is exempt from the firstborn because of the mother, which is the gentile’s, and the seller is exempt because of the offspring, which is the gentile’s. And from two verses it is derived that a gentile’s partnership exempts from the firstborn, even [a share in] its ear, as we say below (Bekhorot 3a): What is different? In it [the offspring] we require “every firstborn” (Numbers 3:13), and that is not the case; its mother too, we require “all your livestock that is male” (Exodus 34:19), and that is not the case. And the reason the Gemara argues that the purchaser and the seller are each necessary, and does not simply say that they are derived from two verses: because the mishna does not teach both [the fetus and the mother] under the purchaser or under the seller. Learn from it that the purchaser and the seller are each needed, as it goes on to explain, since from the purchaser we would not learn the seller; for it could have taught: one who purchases the fetus of a gentile’s animal or the mother; one who sells the fetus to a gentile or the mother. [One might object that] the mishna implies they are both derived from one verse, as it teaches: “exempt, as it is stated: in Israel.” One must say that this refers to the seller, since that whole passage deals not with the mother but only with the fetus.
tosafot:a1.2: In brief: The Sifra (Torat Kohanim, Emor) derives that the firstborn applies to a partnership [of Jews] from the plural “the firstborn of your herds and of your flocks” (Deuteronomy 12:6). Tosafot asks: why not derive it from the fact that “in Israel” was needed to exclude a partnership with a gentile, which implies that a partnership of Jews is obligated? And further: in Chullin 135b (Reishit HaGez) the Gemara says that “your herd and your flock” is needed to exclude a partnership with a gentile, whereas here it is excluded from “in Israel.” Answer: according to what Tosafot explained [in the previous note], there are two verses, one about the fetus and one about the mother. From “in Israel” we exclude a gentile’s partnership in the fetus, and from “your herd” a gentile’s partnership in the mother. The same could have been derived from “all your livestock that is male,” but in Chullin the Gemara preferred to cite “your herd” because it cites “your herds and your flocks” there, as it says: although it is written “your herd and your flock,” one might say: only what is yours, and a partnership the Merciful One did not write; [hence the plural] “your herds and your flocks.” Below (3a) it cites “all your livestock” because of the exposition of “all.” And it is well that the plural “your herds” is needed for a Jewish partnership in the mother: from “in Israel,” which excludes a gentile’s partnership, we would not include a Jewish partnership in the mother, since that verse is written about the offspring. One cannot explain instead that since the verse revealed “in Israel” regarding the offspring, we learn that “your herd” comes to exclude a gentile’s partnership and “in Israel” stands for all the mitzvot: for in all the cases in Chullin 135b where a gentile’s partnership is excluded (teruma from “the first of your grain,” pe’a from “the corner of your field,” tithe from “the tithe of your grain”) it is excluded although “in Israel” is not written there. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a3.1: He brings it to sanctity: Rashi explained: that it will rest on Shabbat; and likewise “he abrogates its sanctity”: that the gentile does labor with it on Shabbat. But the expression “sanctity” does not imply this; rather, it means the sanctity of the firstborn, as in the case of Rav Mari bar Raḥel (3b), whose animals all died because he removed them from sanctity, transferring ownership of their ears to a gentile. And although for a purchaser, if the offspring is male, “he brings it to sanctity” does not apply, sometimes the fetus is female, and he brings it to the sanctity of the firstborn, since the offspring of this fetus will be sanctified as a firstborn. And even without the reason “he brings it to sanctity,” the Gemara could have said that there is no reason to penalize him since there is no abrogation, unlike the seller, where there is abrogation; but it preferred to say that there is even a bringing of sanctity. And it could also have given another reason: had the mishna taught only the purchaser, [he is exempt] because he committed no prohibition; but the seller, who committed a prohibition, as it teaches “although he is not permitted,” I would say let us penalize him. The Gemara took one of the two reasons. And all the more so it is well now that it did not give here the reason I explained on the mishna, that they are derived from two verses.
tosafot:a4.1: To exclude the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda: even without Rabbi Yehuda, it would have been necessary to teach us partnership, since we do not learn it from the first clause; but it was all the more necessary, since we find a dispute about this case.
tosafot:a8.1: But a fetus, since that is its natural state, is not damaged: meaning that people would come to confuse it with another animal. And the Gemara could also have said: because it will in the future be born and become fit for labor, for by this reason we conclude [below] that it is prohibited, as it says: “and this fetus too is like one that is able to be cured.” It took one of the two reasons.
tosafot:a12.1: And he gives half its value to the priest: it is not sanctified with inherent sanctity, to be offered on the altar, because of the gentile’s share, as Rashi explained. And at the end of the chapter (3b) Rabbi Yehuda permits it in shearing and in labor, as he expounds: “You shall do no work with the firstborn of your ox” (Deuteronomy 15:19), but you may work with one that is yours and others’; “nor shear the firstborn of your flock,” but you may shear one that is yours and others’. And if you will say: granted that it is not sanctified with inherent sanctity, nevertheless, since by Torah law it is obligated in the firstborn, the share he has in it should belong to the priest; why does he give the priest the value of his share? One can say: for the priest’s benefit, since a partnership with a gentile does not suit him, as he cannot remove his share from the gentile’s hand so quickly. And as for the latter clause, which teaches “they penalize him up to ten times its value”: if it deals with a firstborn donkey, it is easier to understand, in both the first and the latter clause, that he gives its value, since the firstborn donkey itself is not given to the priest but is redeemed with any lamb or with its value, as stated below (Bekhorot 9a).
tosafot:a12.2: They penalize him up to ten times its value: they penalized specifically for large livestock. But for small livestock, since there is no prohibition but merely a custom, in a place where they are suspected of bestiality, as a gentile has compassion on his own animal that it not become barren, they did not penalize, even in a place where they were not accustomed to sell. And below (3a) Reish Lakish says: one who sells large livestock to a gentile, they penalize him up to ten times its value: specifically large livestock, but not small.
gershom:a1.1: [Rabbeinu Gershom opens with a prayer:] Creator and Former of the lights, who sees and listens to prayers: make me wise to understand sayings acquired of old for the generations, and strengthen me to explain the fine points of Bekhorot.
gershom:a2.1: One who purchases the fetus of his donkey: the firstborn of a gentile’s donkey, while it is still in its mother’s womb.
gershom:a3.1: And one who sells to him: or a Jew who sells the fetus of his donkey to a gentile.
gershom:a4.1: Although he is not permitted: as we say in tractate Avoda Zara, that one does not sell large livestock to gentiles.
gershom:a5.1: And one who enters into a partnership with him: or one who gives a gentile half of his donkey in partnership.
gershom:a6.1: Or one who receives: from a gentile, to look after his donkey, so that half of its fetuses will be his; or a Jew who gives his donkey to a gentile in receivership, so that the offspring will be his [the gentile’s] for a half, a third or a quarter: it is exempt from the firstborn.
gershom:a7.1: As it is stated: “I sanctified to Me every firstborn in Israel”: that is to say, it must be entirely from a Jew, so that a gentile has no share in it. And the Gemara explains in the other chapter: why does the tanna teach the fetus of his donkey first, and then teach the fetus of his cow? Let it teach the fetus of a cow first, etc.
gershom:a8.1: Why do I need all these: the purchaser, the seller, the one who enters a partnership, the one who receives and the one who gives.
gershom:a9.1: Because he brings it to sanctity: in that no labor is done with it on Shabbat. Therefore they were lenient with the one who purchases a fetus, that that fetus itself is exempt from the firstborn. But one who sells the fetus of his donkey, as he removes it from the sanctity of Shabbat and of the firstborn, say that they should penalize him, that he give its redemption to the priest. It teaches us that they do not.
gershom:a10.1: And why do I need one who enters into a partnership with him? Now, the purchaser, where the entire fetus is the Jew’s, is exempt; the partner, who has only half of it, need it be stated?
gershom:a11.1: It comes to teach us this, to exclude the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda: he did not say it explicitly, but this is what he says below: Rabbi Yehuda says: one who receives an animal from a gentile; which is a partnership, as he receives it to fatten it and to divide the offspring.
gershom:a12.1: Lest it be confused with another animal: that another person, who sees that this one does not redeem the fetus of his donkey, says: so too I need not redeem the firstborn of my donkey; for he does not know that this one did not redeem the firstborn of his donkey because he gave it to a gentile in receivership.
gershom:a13.1: You might say: let us penalize him to redeem it, so that it not come to be confused. It teaches us that we do not.
gershom:a14.1: We learned there: this is the first clause of that mishna: one does not sell large livestock to gentiles, calves or foals, and it lists all of them, and it teaches: Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a damaged one, since it is not fit for labor; and ben Beteira permits a horse, since one does not do with it labor for which one is liable to a sin-offering, for a horse ordinarily stands for riding, and riding is prohibited only by rabbinic decree, since a living being carries itself.
gershom:a15.1: A fetus while it is in its mother’s womb, what does Rabbi Yehuda, who permits a damaged one, say? Is it permitted to sell this fetus to a gentile or not?
gershom:a16.1: Because it is damaged: and it is not fit for labor.
gershom:a17.1: A fetus too is damaged: with respect to labor.
gershom:a18.1: Or perhaps: he permits a damaged one for this reason, that this is not its natural state, as it is not the way of an animal to be damaged; and so when it is damaged it is permitted to sell it to a gentile.
gershom:a19.1: But a fetus, that is its natural state: it is like a damaged one, in that it is damaged in its mother’s womb, and while it is small it is not fit for labor; but it is not truly like a damaged one, since it will become fit for labor when it grows up. So let us say that Rabbi Yehuda prohibits it.
gershom:a20.1: And Rabbi Yehuda does not disagree in the mishna: by inference, he too holds that one is not permitted to sell a fetus to a gentile.
gershom:a21.1: That it does not teach that Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: and would it enter your mind that he does not disagree about them? But there is a place where he disagrees, as we say below: Rabbi Yehuda says: one who receives an animal from a gentile and it gave birth, they assess it, etc.; [so for him an animal of] partners with a gentile is obligated in the firstborn. Rather, he disagrees about partners, and the same is true of all of them; and if the mishna does not teach the dispute, he disagrees in a baraita. And since he disagrees, learn from it that according to Rabbi Yehuda it is permitted to sell a fetus to a gentile.
gershom:a22.1: They assess it at its worth: they appraise that offspring, how much it is worth, and he gives half its value to the priest, the half that is his.
gershom:a23.1: Although he is not permitted to give it to a gentile in receivership: because the gentile does labor with it on Shabbat, and furthermore because he removes it from the firstborn.
gershom:a24.1: They penalize him up to ten, etc.: that he must redeem the fetus from the gentile, even if he cannot redeem it from the gentile unless he gives him ten parts beyond its value.
gershom:b1.1: And he gives the value of the fetus to the priest: and although it is written “you shall redeem with a lamb” (Exodus 13:13), he may redeem it even with money, as we say in the other chapter, for the Torah came not to be stringent with him but to be lenient with him. But other firstborns, of a kosher animal, are not redeemed with money; rather, he gives the firstborn to the priest, and if the priest wishes to sell it to him, he may. And what is the reason he gives all its value to the priest, and half its value does not suffice? Because the primary animal is the Jew’s.
gershom:b2.1: What, is it not: that which it teaches “they penalize,” does it not refer to the fetus, and because “he is not permitted”? Evidently Rabbi Yehuda holds that it is prohibited to sell a fetus to a gentile, since that is its natural state.
gershom:b3.1: It refers to the animal: that they penalize him for it; but a fetus he is permitted to sell.
gershom:b4.1: But it teaches “up to ten times its value [damav]”: which implies the value of the fetus.
gershom:b5.1: Teach “its value [dameha]”: which implies the value of the animal.
gershom:b6.1: And if you wish to say it refers to the animal, [read] “all its [the animal’s] value.”
gershom:b7.1: What is the relevance of the priest to the animal itself? Why does he give him all its value? Rather, is it not referring to the fetus?
gershom:b8.1: No: actually he holds in general that one may sell a fetus to a gentile, as it is like a damaged one. And here, what is different, that it teaches “they penalize,” which implies the fetus as well? For example, where he gave a gentile a pregnant animal to fatten, so that when it is fattened they will sell it and divide its value; now they penalize him for the animal itself, and since they penalize him, etc. And this is “and he gives all its value to the priest.” But in general it is permitted to sell [a fetus] to a gentile.
gershom:b9.1: And this too is like one that is able to be cured, for when it grows up it is fit for labor. Learn from it that according to Rabbi Yehuda it is prohibited to sell a fetus to a gentile.
gershom:b10.1: There are those who teach it: this statement of Rabbi Yehuda, as referring to the mishna, and they do not raise it as a dilemma.
gershom:b11.1: Let us say the mishna is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: for since Rabbi Yehuda permits a damaged one, the same is true that he permits a fetus too, as it is like a damaged one.
gershom:b12.1: You may even say it is Rabbi Yehuda: and it is a damaged one that he permits, since that is not its natural state, as he said above; but a fetus he prohibits, since it is its natural state to be like a damaged one while it is in its mother’s womb, but in the end it is fit for labor; so it is prohibited.
gershom:b13.1: He sold an animal: that is not pregnant, to a gentile, for its fetuses, so that the fetuses will belong to both of them.
gershom:b14.1: Let it be raised according to both of them: for here he sells neither the animal itself nor a fetus, since it is not yet pregnant.
gershom:b15.1: A damaged one, which will not be confused with a whole one.
gershom:b16.1: But a whole one: where he sold an animal for its fetuses, and the animal itself is whole, it will come to be confused with another sale of a whole animal, sold outright and not for its fetuses; so he prohibits it.
gershom:b17.1: Or perhaps: if a damaged one, which is separated from him, as he sells it outright to the gentile, although there is concern for confusion with another outright sale of a whole one, is even so permitted,
gershom:b18.1: then all the more so a whole one sold for its fetuses, which is not separated from him, as he does not sell it entirely, is permitted. Or perhaps, according to the Rabbis: if a damaged one, which will not be confused with a whole one, the Rabbis even so prohibit, lest one come to confuse an outright sale of a whole one with the outright sale of this one, then all the more so a whole one sold for its fetuses, which will come to be confused, a whole one with a whole one, and one should be concerned for an outright sale. And it entered the Gemara’s mind that whoever prohibits an animal sold for its fetuses, lest it be confused with another animal sold outright, likewise also prohibits selling it to a gentile for its shearing and its milk, since there too one can say: lest one come to confuse this sale of a whole one with another whole one sold outright.
gershom:b19.1: And is the reason of the Rabbis because of this? Can you say that the Rabbis prohibit a whole one because it will come to be confused? Does their reason depend on confusion?
gershom:b20.1: They said to Rabbi Yehuda: why do you permit a damaged one? But don’t they breed it and it gives birth, and it turns out that he sold him a whole large animal? Evidently the reason of the Rabbis who prohibit is because of the fetus, since it is prohibited to sell a fetus to a gentile, and not because of confusion; and since we are concerned not about confusion but only about the fetus, learn from it that a damaged one sold for its shearing and its milk is permitted. But actually the reason of the Rabbis is that they are concerned about confusion, and for that reason they prohibit selling for shearing and milk, and this is what they are saying to him, etc.: What is the reason you permit a damaged one? It is like one who sold it to him for slaughter, since he will kill it immediately, and no one will know that he sold it to a gentile, and one will not come to confuse an outright sale with an outright sale, since he kills it immediately and it is no longer extant. But certainly one cannot say that he kills it immediately, for doesn’t he keep it in order to breed it, so that it gives birth? And since he keeps it, one will come to confuse it with an outright sale. So why do you permit it, since he does not kill it?
gershom:b21.1: And Rabbi Yehuda said to them: when it gives birth. That is to say, when you see any damaged animal in the world that gives birth, then ask me why I permit a damaged one; for certainly it does not give birth.
gershom:b22.1: For it does not accept a male: because it is damaged and cannot bear him. Therefore Rabbi Yehuda permits it, as he is not concerned that the gentile might keep it for the sake of offspring. But a whole one sold for its fetuses, according to Rabbi Yehuda, is still a dilemma for you.
gershom:b23.1: And it does not teach regarding one who gives it to him in receivership “although he is not permitted”: since it does not teach this, learn from it that the Rabbis hold that one who sells an animal for its fetus [is permitted], for receivership is for half the improvement and the offspring, and this is an animal sold for its fetuses.
gershom:b24.1: And according to your reasoning, one who enters into a partnership: where it does not teach “although he is not permitted,” so too is he permitted to enter a partnership?
gershom:b25.1: “Neither let it be heard out of your mouth”: that you not ask with your mouth that he swear to you by his idol.
gershom:b26.1: Rather, it teaches regarding a sale “although he is not permitted,” and the same is true for partnership: that he is not permitted to enter a partnership with him; and the same is true for receivership, that he is not permitted to give him an animal in receivership, since according to the Rabbis one who sells an animal for its fetus is prohibited.
gershom:b27.1: And what is different about a sale, that it chose it: that regarding a sale it teaches “although he is not permitted”? Because the primary prohibition is in a sale; therefore it teaches regarding it that he is not permitted, and the same is true for all of them.
gershom:b28.1: [As long as] the gentile’s hand is in the middle: that he has some share in it.
rashi:a3.1: GEMARA. He brings it to sanctity: that it will rest on Shabbat; and since he is performing a mitzva, there is no reason to penalize him.
rashi:a3.2: Say: let us penalize him: to redeem the fetus from the gentile and give it to the priest.
rashi:a4.1: To exclude the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda: who says below: one who receives an animal from a gentile, they assess it at its worth and he gives half its value to the priest.
rashi:a6.1: And the primary animal: the body of the animal and half the offspring.
rashi:a6.2: Lest it be confused with another animal: in which the gentile has no share, neither in it nor in its offspring, and one would come to exempt that one too from the firstborn.
rashi:a7.1: We learned there: in tractate Avoda Zara (14b).
rashi:a7.2: Rabbi Yehuda permits a damaged one: to sell to a gentile an animal whose legs are broken, and in a place where they are not suspected of bestiality. And ben Beteira permits a horse, since one does not do with it labor that carries liability for a sin-offering, for an ordinary horse stands for riding, and one who rides on Shabbat [transgresses] only a rabbinic prohibition, since a living being carries itself.
rashi:a8.1: A fetus, what would Rabbi Yehuda say to me: about selling it to a gentile, is it permitted or prohibited?
rashi:a8.2: Because it is damaged: and it is not fit for labor.
rashi:a8.3: And a fetus too is damaged: with respect to labor.
rashi:a8.4: Or perhaps damaged, that is not its natural state: for an animal to be damaged; therefore it is something unusual, and people will not come to confuse it and permit selling a whole one.
rashi:a9.1: Come and hear: [the mishna,] which deals with a fetus and teaches “he is not permitted,” because of labor on Shabbat.
rashi:a10.1: And according to your reasoning, one who enters into a partnership with him: which the mishna teaches regarding the firstborn, that it is exempt, and it does not teach “Rabbi Yehuda obligates”; so too [would you say] that he does not disagree? But we see below in this passage that he disagrees in that baraita.
rashi:a12.1: Rabbi Yehuda says: one who receives an animal, etc., and it gave birth: to a firstborn.
rashi:a12.3: And he gives half its value to the priest: but it is not sanctified with inherent sanctity, to be offered on the altar, since half of it belongs to the gentile.
rashi:a12.4: And one who gives it to him in receivership: this too is not sanctified with inherent sanctity, since half of it is the gentile’s; it is exempt from the firstborn. And that he gives all its value to the priest is a penalty, as they penalize him because he sold it to a gentile. And “one who gives it to him in receivership although he is not permitted”: that is to say, although he is not permitted to give it to a gentile even as a gift.
rashi:a12.5: They penalize him: since he paid no heed to the words of the Sages.
tosafot:b1.1: What, is it not referring to the fetus: meaning, and it deals with a pregnant animal. No, to the animal: meaning, and it does not deal with a fetus but with an animal sold for its fetus. And so it is implied below, regarding the dilemma “an animal sold for its fetuses, what is the halakha?”, where the Gemara seeks to resolve from here that it is prohibited, saying “What, is it not referring to the animal?” Learn from it that if it refers to the animal, it deals with an animal sold for its fetus. But seemingly it does not deal with an animal sold for its fetus, for if so, what is the challenge “but it teaches its value [damav]”? Let us say it refers to the fetus [to come]. And if you say that it seemed to the Gemara to refer to the animal, then below too let it infer so. Rather, here it deals with an animal given for fattening, as the Gemara concludes, [and below] with an animal sold for its fetus.
tosafot:b17.1: For it does not accept a male: not because of being a tereifa [which cannot give birth], since it is said in Chullin 57b (Elu Tereifot), regarding Rabbi Shimon ben Ḥalafta, who was an investigator of things: “And perhaps Rabbi Yehuda holds that a tereifa gives birth and thrives.” Some books do not read “gives birth” there, as there is no need there for giving birth, only for thriving. In any case, it is reasonable here that Rabbi Yehuda permits even [an animal broken] from the knee down, because it does not accept a male.
tosafot:b19.1: And according to your reasoning, one who enters into a partnership with him, etc.: regarding receivership it is not apt to challenge that it should be prohibited because of partnership, since receivership does not lead to an oath so much. And the Gemara specifically took partnership; but other commerce is not prohibited.
tosafot:b19.2: It is prohibited for a person to enter into a partnership with a gentile: what is taught in the first chapter of Avoda Zara (22a), a Jew and a gentile who received a field in partnership; and likewise the case where the gentile takes the years of orla and the Jew takes the permitted years; and what is said in Chullin 133a (HaZero’a), one who enters into a partnership with a gentile must mark [his share]: all these disagree with Shmuel’s father.
tosafot:b19.3: Lest the gentile become obligated to take an oath to him: from here Rabbeinu Shmuel prohibits accepting an oath [from a gentile], by an a fortiori inference. Rabbeinu Tam permits it, since it is like rescuing [one’s money] from them, as is taught in the first chapter of Avoda Zara (6b): a loan by word of mouth may be collected from them [on their festival], because it is like rescuing it from them, even though he goes and gives thanks [to his idol]. One can distinguish, though, between a possibility and a certainty. Rabbeinu Tam further brings proof from the last chapter of Megilla (28a), where Avuh bar Ihi said: “May [a reward] come to me, for I never made a partnership with a gentile”: if it were prohibited, what was his special merit? And likewise Rabbeinu Tam explained that people were not careful about the three Shabbat meals, since it says in Shabbat 118b: “May [a reward] come to me, for I kept three meals,” implying that not everyone was careful about them. Rabbeinu Tam further explained that nowadays they all swear by their holy objects and do not treat them as divinity; and although they mention the name of Heaven with them and intend something else, nevertheless this is not the name of idolatry, as their intention is to the Maker of heaven and earth. And although they associate the name of Heaven with something else, there is no [violation of] “Before the blind do not place a stumbling block” (Leviticus 19:14), for the descendants of Noah were not warned about this; and as for us, we find no prohibition in causing such association.
tosafot:b20.1: That the primary one is a sale: Rashi explained that the primary prohibition is the sale, meaning that he wants to say the primary prohibition is the sale. But it is difficult: partnership is not prohibited because of a sale, but because of what Shmuel’s father said. One must say: the primary, straightforward prohibition is a sale, as we learned in the first chapter of Avoda Zara (14b).
rashi:b1.1: What, is it not referring to the fetus: when it says “he is not permitted”?
rashi:b2.1: What is the relevance of the priest: to the animal? Rather, certainly it refers to the fetus.
rashi:b2.2: No: actually, do not resolve the question from here, for here, with what are we dealing? For example, where he gave him a pregnant animal to fatten and to take half the improvement, both in the fattening and in the offspring; since we penalize him, etc. But if he sold him the fetus alone, no.
rashi:b3.1: That cannot be cured: and do labor on Shabbat.
rashi:b4.1: Permits a damaged one: and a fetus is similar to a damaged one.
rashi:b5.1: That is its natural state: and it is not damaged.
rashi:b9.1: An animal for its fetuses: for example, where it is not yet pregnant, and he sold him all the offspring that it will conceive in the future, but the animal itself he did not sell him.
rashi:b9.2: What is the halakha: is he penalized and made to redeem it, because of [the prohibition on] one who sells an animal to a gentile?
rashi:b10.1: That people will come to confuse: and permit selling a whole one.
rashi:b11.1: Which is separated from him: as he retained nothing in it for himself once he sold it.
rashi:b11.2: And all the more so an unblemished one: in such a case, which is not separated from him, since he retained the body of the animal for himself; and as for the fetuses, there is no concern, since it has not yet conceived and he sold him nothing, and when they come, they come into being in the gentile’s domain.
rashi:b12.1: As it is separated from him: and it is an outright sale, and people will come to confuse it and permit an outright sale of a whole one. But here, where it is not separated from him, it is permitted, as it is not a sale.
rashi:b13.1: And all the more so an unblemished one, which people may come to confuse: with an outright sale of another whole one.
rashi:b14.1: Is it for this reason: said in astonishment, that we needed to raise the dilemma.
rashi:b14.2: With it: with the damaged one.
rashi:b14.3: Apparently: the reason of the Rabbis is because of the fetuses. Resolve from it that according to the Rabbis it is prohibited to sell an animal to a gentile for its fetuses, and according to Rabbi Yehuda it is permitted. [The answer:] Actually, the reason of the Rabbis is because of confusion, and it was necessary to raise the dilemma, since, as it is not separated from him, one can say that people will not come to confuse it with a complete sale. And this is what the Rabbis are saying to Rabbi Yehuda.
rashi:b15.1: It is like one who sold it for slaughter: and there is no concern about confusion, since whoever sees it knows that he sold it to him only for slaughter, and will not come to sell an animal not for slaughter.
rashi:b16.1: He delays it: for the sake of the offspring, and one who sees it in the gentile’s house at the end of a year or two thinks it is permitted to sell an animal to a gentile not for slaughter.
rashi:b18.1: Come and hear: from the mishna.
rashi:b18.2: And it does not teach “although he is not permitted”: evidently it is permitted to sell an animal for its fetuses, since receivership is a sale for the fetuses, as the gentile shares only in the offspring; for the Gemara assumed that the gentile does not share in the improvement from fattening the animal.
rashi:b19.1: Out of your mouth: by your mouth’s causing it.
rashi:b20.1: It taught that a sale: is not permitted, and the same is true for all of them.
rashi:b20.2: And what is different about a sale, that it cited: “he is not permitted” regarding it, and did not cite it with one of these others?
rashi:b20.3: That the primary prohibition is a sale: the primary prohibition is the sale of an animal.
